Lesson 10

Jev and System One models

A model that answers typed questions with a probability for every option, instead of writing text. TypeSafe's Jev through its official SDK, and a local Jev-like adapter over Ollama that speaks the same API (simulated: there is no local Jev), scored against a keyword rule and an LLM that writes JSON on 30 labelled fake support tickets: accuracy, typed answers, Brier score and wrong pages at 3 a.m. Your policy turns the probabilities into actions. Python, Node.js and C#; the demo installs nothing.

↓ Download lesson PDF ↓ Download slide deck PDF · downloadable
Follow along in:
Overview

What you'll build

New to System One models? A chat model writes text. A System One model answers typed questions - yes/no, pick one, rate on a scale - with a probability for every option, in one pass. Nothing to parse; the answer cannot be anything but an option you defined. Jev is TypeSafe's System One model.

There is no local Jev: TypeSafe serves it only as a hosted API. So this lesson calls the real Jev through TypeSafe's official SDK when you bring a key, and builds a local Jev-like adapter - labelled simulated - that answers the same API with a local model through Ollama. Then it scores four engines on 30 labelled fake support tickets and asks the course's question: what does each one buy, and what does it cost? Pick a language above and press -> to begin.

   Lesson 9's model chose an action. Here the model only answers; your code decides.

   Four engines, one API (POST /v1/systemone), one scorecard:
     keywords            rules, no model

     Jev-like adapter    a local model answers one letter per question (simulated)

   30 labelled fake tickets. Accuracy, typed answers, Brier score, wrong pages.
Setup

What you need

Nothing to install for the demo. It replays answers recorded from real runs, so it needs no model and prints the same thing on every machine, in Python, Node.js and C#. For the live actions you need [Ollama](https://ollama.com/download) and qwen3:1.7b. For the real Jev you need a key from [console.typesafe.ai](https://console.typesafe.ai) and the official SDK, pinned with hashes. Run everything from the repo root:

run
$ ./run -l 10                       # Python: the playground (default)
./run -l 10 demo                  # four engines, one scorecard - offline
./run -l 10 --lang node demo      # the same scorecard from Node.js
./run -l 10 --lang csharp demo    # and from C#
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b            # only for the live actions
Step 1

A question is a type and a sentence

Four questions per ticket, written in TypeSafe's own request format: a choice (which queue), a score (urgency, five ordered levels) and two noul yes/no questions. The criteria are what the model reads to tell the options apart.

The options are the output. A System One model cannot answer "very high" to a question whose levels are none..critical; an LLM asked to write JSON can, and this lesson counts how often it does.
Step 2

The whole API: one POST

POST /v1/systemone with {model, state, questions} and a Bearer key. The standard library is enough; the official SDK does the same with retries and types.

python/systemone.py
def post(base_url: str, body: dict, api_key: str = "", timeout: float = 120.0) -> tuple[dict, float]:
    """POST one request; return (response, seconds).

    A key is only ever sent to TypeSafe or to this machine: anything else is refused,
    so a typo in TYPESAFE_BASE_URL cannot hand the key (or the tickets) to a stranger.
    """
    if not (base_url.rstrip("/") == TYPESAFE_URL or is_loopback(base_url)):
        raise ValueError(f"refusing {base_url}: only {TYPESAFE_URL} or a loopback address")
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        base_url.rstrip("/") + SYSTEM_ONE_PATH,
        data=json.dumps(body).encode("utf-8"),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json",
                 **({"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"} if api_key else {})},
    )
    started = time.monotonic()
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as resp:
            data = json.load(resp)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as err:
        detail = err.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")[:300]
        raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {err.code} from {base_url}: {detail}") from None
    except (urllib.error.URLError, socket.timeout) as err:
        raise RuntimeError(f"cannot reach {base_url}: {err}") from None
    return data, time.monotonic() - started
The function refuses any destination except https://api.typesafe.ai or a loopback address. A typo in TYPESAFE_BASE_URL cannot send your key - or your tickets - to a stranger.
Step 3

Every answer becomes a label and a probability

read_answers() turns the three wire shapes into one: {pick, probs, confidence}, keyed by label. A noul's 0.93 becomes {yes: 0.93, no: 0.07}; a score's {"2": 0.7} becomes {medium: 0.7}.

python/systemone.py
def read_answers(questions: dict, response: dict) -> tuple[dict, list[str]]:
    """Turn a wire response into {question: {"pick", "probs", "confidence"}}.

    Every pick is a label from `options()` ("yes"/"no" for a noul, the level name for
    a score), so the caller compares labels and never cares about the wire shape.
    A question with a missing or malformed answer is left out and reported.
    """
    answers, problems = {}, []
    got = response.get("answers") or {}
    for name, q in questions.items():
        a = got.get(name)
        labels = options(q)
        if not isinstance(a, dict) or a.get("type") != q["type"]:
            problems.append(f"{name}: no {q['type']} answer")
            continue
        if q["type"] == "noul":
            p = a.get("noul")
            if not isinstance(p, (int, float)) or not 0 <= p <= 1:
                problems.append(f"{name}: noul must be a number in [0, 1]")
                continue
            probs = {"yes": float(p), "no": 1.0 - float(p)}
            pick = "yes" if p >= 0.5 else "no"
            confidence = max(p, 1 - p)
        else:
            raw = a.get("probabilities")
            raw = raw if isinstance(raw, dict) else {}
            if q["type"] == "score":
                raw = {labels[int(k)]: v for k, v in raw.items()
                       if isinstance(k, str) and k.isascii() and k.isdigit() and int(k) < len(labels)}
            numeric = all(isinstance(v, (int, float)) and not isinstance(v, bool) for v in raw.values())
            if set(raw) != set(labels) or not numeric or abs(fsum(raw.values()) - 1.0) > 0.01:
                problems.append(f"{name}: probabilities must cover {labels} and sum to 1")
                continue
            probs = {label: float(raw[label]) for label in labels}
            pick = a.get("choice") if q["type"] == "choice" else max(labels, key=probs.get)
            if pick not in labels:
                problems.append(f"{name}: {pick!r} is not an option")
                continue
            confidence = a.get("confidence")
            if not isinstance(confidence, (int, float)) or isinstance(confidence, bool):
                confidence = max(probs.values())
            confidence = float(confidence)
        answers[name] = {"pick": pick, "probs": probs, "confidence": confidence}
    return answers, problems
Everything downstream - the policy, the scorecard, the playground - sees one shape, so it cannot tell TypeSafe's Jev from the local adapter or from the keyword rules. That is what makes the comparison fair.
Step 4

TypeSafeClient() reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Leave the URL unset and it calls TypeSafe's Jev; set it to http://127.0.0.1:8765 and the same code calls the local adapter. Node.js has the same in node/sdk_example.mjs.

Install it with ./run -l 10 install-sdk: every file is checked against a sha256 in requirements-sdk.txt, into its own venv. On npm, npm audit signatures verifies the package was built from TypeSafe's GitHub repository. And pip install qev installs an unrelated project - not anything from TypeSafe.
Step 5

Making a local LLM answer like Jev

Each question becomes a lettered multiple-choice prompt, with the ticket fenced as data and an instruction to ignore instructions inside it (Lesson 4).

python/local_adapter.py
def prompt_for(state, question: dict) -> list[dict]:
    """The chat messages for one question. The option texts are the criteria."""
    labels = systemone.options(question)
    criteria = question.get("criteria")
    if question["type"] == "noul":
        texts = [criteria.get("true", "yes"), criteria.get("false", "no")] if criteria else ["yes", "no"]
        texts = [f"yes - {texts[0]}", f"no - {texts[1]}"]
    elif question["type"] == "choice":
        texts = [f"{label} - {desc}" if desc else label for label, desc in criteria.items()]
    else:
        texts = list(labels)
    lines = "\n".join(f"{LETTERS[i]}) {t}" for i, t in enumerate(texts))
    shown = state if isinstance(state, str) else json.dumps(state, ensure_ascii=False)
    return [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Input:\n<<<\n{shown}\n>>>\n\n"
                                        f"Question: {question['instructions']}\n{lines}\n\n"
                                        f"Answer with one letter."}]
This is the simulated part. The adapter serves the same API, so the SDK works against it unchanged, but the model was never trained for this. It is a way to learn the idea locally, not a stand-in for Jev's quality.
Step 6

One token, a probability per option

The model may write exactly one token. Ollama returns the log-probabilities of the top 20 candidates for it; each option gets the probability of its letter, renormalised. One short forward pass per question.

python/local_adapter.py
def letter_probabilities(top_logprobs: list[dict], n: int) -> list[float]:
    """Probability per option letter from the first token's top candidates.

    "A", " A" and "a" are the same answer. Letters outside the top 20 get 0. If no
    option letter appears at all, every option gets an equal share - the honest
    answer to "the model said something else".
    """
    mass = [0.0] * n
    for cand in top_logprobs:
        token = cand.get("token", "").strip().upper()
        if len(token) == 1 and token in LETTERS[:n]:
            mass[LETTERS.index(token)] += math.exp(cand.get("logprob", -1e9))
    total = sum(mass)
    if total <= 0:
        return [1.0 / n] * n
    return [m / total for m in mass]
Jev answers up to 64 questions in one pass. The adapter needs one call per question - four per ticket here - and a small model is often 100% sure and wrong. The scorecard measures both.
Step 7

The model answers; your policy decides

Three thresholds and no model: PAGE, REFUND, CONFIDENT. The model never says "page on-call". It says P(high or critical) = 0.83, and this code decides that is enough.

python/policy.py
def decide(answers: dict, page: float = PAGE, refund: float = REFUND,
           confident: float = CONFIDENT) -> str:
    """One action per ticket, from the answers to the four ticket questions."""
    queue = answers.get("queue")
    if queue is None:
        return "human triage"  # no usable answer: never guess
    urgency = answers.get("urgency", {}).get("probs", {})
    p_urgent = urgency.get("high", 0.0) + urgency.get("critical", 0.0)
    p_refund = answers.get("refund_request", {}).get("probs", {}).get("yes", 0.0)
    p_human = answers.get("needs_human", {}).get("probs", {}).get("yes", 1.0)

    if queue["probs"].get("trust_safety", 0.0) >= 0.5:
        return "escalate: trust & safety"
    if p_urgent >= page and queue["pick"] == "technical":
        return "page on-call"
    if p_refund >= refund and queue["pick"] == "billing":
        return "draft refund for approval"
    if p_human >= 0.5 or queue["confidence"] < confident:
        return "human triage"
    return "auto-route"
Move a threshold and the behaviour changes without retraining or re-prompting anything. That only works when the probabilities mean something: rules and JSON answers are always 0 or 1, so for them the knob does nothing.
Step 8

What goes wrong when an LLM writes the answer

The usual way: ask a chat model for JSON, then parse it. Every value that is not one of the options is a type error, and the question goes unanswered.

python/engines.py
def parse_llm_json(body: dict, text: str) -> tuple[dict, list[str]]:
    """Read what the model wrote. Anything that is not a valid option is a type error.

    Returns (response, errors). A field the model got wrong, or left out, is simply
    missing from the response: the scorecard counts it as unanswered.
    """
    errors = []
    match = re.search(r"\{.*\}", text, re.S)
    try:
        written = json.loads(match.group(0)) if match else None
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        written = None
    if not isinstance(written, dict):
        return {"model": "llm-json", "answers": {}, "usage": {}}, ["not a JSON object"]
    answers = {}
    for name, q in body["questions"].items():
        value = written.get(name)
        if isinstance(value, bool):  # {"refund_request": true} is a fair reading
            value = "yes" if value else "no"
        if not isinstance(value, str) or value.strip().lower() not in systemone.options(q):
            errors.append(f"{name}={value!r}")
            continue
        answers[name] = certain(q, value.strip().lower())
    return {"model": "llm-json", "answers": answers, "usage": {}}, errors
This is the comparison that matters most in practice. Same model, same tickets: written answers can be invalid and carry no probability; letter probabilities are always valid and can be thresholded.
Step 9

Scoring a decision: the Brier score

The squared distance between the probabilities and the truth. 0 is perfect; certain and wrong costs 2 per question; "no idea" on a yes/no question costs 0.5.

python/scorecard.py
def brier(question: dict, answer: dict | None, truth: str) -> float:
    labels = systemone.options(question)
    if answer is None:
        probs = {label: 1.0 / len(labels) for label in labels}
    else:
        probs = answer["probs"]
    return systemone.fsum((probs[label] - (1.0 if label == truth else 0.0)) ** 2 for label in labels)
Accuracy ranks an engine that is confidently wrong next to one that knows when it is unsure. Only the second lets a threshold do its job. Lesson 5 scored retrieval against a golden set; this is the same discipline for decisions.

Going further

When to use which

Rules when the signal is a word or a number and a miss is cheap. A System One model for a judgement over text, many items, a typed answer and a threshold: ticket routing, moderation, lead scoring, fraud flags, alert severity, and guarding an LLM's output. An LLM when the output is text or the steps are unknown: replies, summaries, agents. Both: the LLM acts, the System One model checks - Jev as the guard on Lesson 9's tool calls, or deciding whether a retrieved passage is an injection (Lesson 4).

Recap

What you learned

A System One model answers typed questions with a probability per option, and your code decides. You called it by hand and through the official SDK, built a local imitation that speaks the same API, and scored four engines on accuracy, typed answers, calibration and the cost at 3 a.m. You saw why the policy must be yours, and why a probability is only useful when it is calibrated.
